claim: Check the Amazon page-one price spread: a tight band like $7 to $13 signals a price war; a $20 to $100 spread means buyers judge on more than price.
body: Search the product's main keyword on Amazon and note every price on page one. When near-identical items cluster in a narrow band, buyers see them as interchangeable and choose on price and review count; any new entrant has to undercut, and margins fall. The example given is tongue scrapers, where page one ran from about $7 to $13, a spread of about $6 that the seller calls a reason to walk away. When the same kind of product sells at $20, $30, $50 and $100 on one page, buyers are paying for differences in design, quality, bundle or brand, which leaves room for a better product at a higher price. How to apply: for each shortlisted candidate, record the lowest and highest price on page one for its main keyword and two or three variant keywords; drop candidates where the top price is less than about double the bottom price, then look at what the top-priced listings do differently and whether you can match it. Use this alongside the price floor and margin floor checks, not in place of them.
conditions: Private-label product selection on Amazon US; comparing listings that serve the same need.
fails_when: The wide spread comes from different products sharing one keyword (pack sizes, unrelated items), not from differentiation; the high-priced listings are established brands you cannot match.

healthy spread example: $20 to $100 for near-identical products

claim: Prefer Amazon products shoppers describe in dozens of ways (slim, waterproof, wallet, for men); one- or two-keyword products leave no cheap long-tail terms to launch on.
body: Amazon search works like a search engine: shoppers type many different descriptions for the same item. A phone case can be searched as slim, waterproof, wallet, green, for men, for women and so on, each a separate search with its own competition. A new listing cannot win the main term early, but it can rank on page one for many smaller descriptive terms, and those cheaper, less contested keywords are what the launch ad campaigns target first. Their combined sales build the velocity that later lifts rank on the main term. Products that are only ever searched with one or two words offer no such side doors: every sale has to come from the most competitive term, at the highest click cost. How to apply: for each candidate, pull the keyword list from a research tool and count distinct descriptive variants with meaningful search volume; favour products with dozens of them; build the launch Sponsored Products campaigns around the long-tail set and track organic rank on each.

claim: Screen out Amazon private-label products under about $25: at an $8 price and $1 per click, two or three clicks per sale erase the profit.
body: On Amazon a new private-label listing pays for most early sales through Sponsored Products clicks, and click cost does not shrink with the product's price. If a click costs about $1 and an $8 item needs two or three clicks to sell once, advertising alone eats the margin before fees and product cost. Cheap products carry two more problems: a low barrier to entry (200 units at $0.75 to $2 each costs a few hundred dollars), which invites price wars, and flimsy quality, which brings bad reviews that sink the listing. The seller in this source, running two US accounts with about $102,000 in sales over 30 days, says his most profitable items all sell above $30, and screens candidates at $25 to $60. He pairs the price floor with a margin floor: at least 30% net margin after landed cost (product, freight, duties, taxes and fees to get stock into Amazon) and FBA fees. How to apply: set the research tool's price filter to $25 to $60; for each candidate estimate clicks per sale (1 divided by conversion rate) times expected cost per click, and check what is left after landed cost and FBA fees; drop anything below 30%.

fails_when: The product sells mostly through organic rank or an outside audience, so little paid traffic is needed; consumables with high repeat purchase that recover acquisition cost later; categories where click costs are far below $1.

claim: Target Amazon products whose current sellers make $5,000 to $20,000 a month; a $30,000-a-month product needs about three months of stock plus heavy launch ad spend.

body: The founder says the brand had the number one best seller badge in deodorant on Amazon before spending anything on Amazon ads, with a reported 6.3% share of the category. He keeps the same price on Amazon as at Sephora and positions the product as an 'everybody brand' rather than a Sephora brand, which also reaches male buyers who rarely shop at Sephora. claim: In manual Sponsored Products campaigns, bid highest on exact match, lower on phrase and lowest on broad, as Amazon Ads recommends, because exact queries are the most relevant and broad buys reach.
body: Amazon Ads' targeting guide defines the three keyword match types. Broad match gives the widest exposure, matching related shopping queries. Exact match matches the search term word for word, same words in the same order. Amazon's own advice for manual bids is to set the highest bid on exact, a lower one on phrase and the lowest on broad. body: Amazon Ads' ACOS guide sets the two efficiency measures for sponsored ads. ACOS (advertising cost of sales) is ad spend divided by ad-attributed revenue, times 100. Amazon says there is no single good ACOS, that ACOS should not be the only metric watched, and that new campaigns often show a high ACOS simply because they are new. claim: TACoS divides ad spend by total sales, organic included: $100 of ads with $100 of ad sales is 100% ACoS, but with $900 organic sales on top it is a 10% TACoS.
body: TACoS (total advertising cost of sales) is a seller-community metric, not one Amazon defines in its ad documentation. Helium 10's explainer gives the formula as advertising spend divided by total revenue, times 100, and contrasts it with ACoS: $100 of spend producing $100 of ad-attributed sales is 100% ACoS, yet if the same product also sold $900 organically, total sales are $1,000 and TACoS is 10%. The point is that ACoS judges a campaign, while TACoS judges how dependent the whole product or store is on advertising. A falling or flat TACoS while sales grow suggests ads are lifting organic rank and sales; a rising TACoS with flat total sales means the business is buying the same revenue at a higher price. The article gives no good TACoS number, so the target has to come from the product's margin. How to apply: track TACoS monthly per ASIN beside ACoS; during launch accept a high ACoS if TACoS trends down as organic sales arrive, and treat a TACoS that keeps rising for several months as the signal to fix the listing or price, not just bids.

claim: Amazon.in bills shipping on actual or volumetric weight (LxBxH cm / 5000), whichever is higher, in 500 g steps; FBA pick and pack is Rs 17 up to 1 kg, storage Rs 50 per cubic foot monthly, plus 18% GST.
body: Amazon India's fees and pricing page sets out how fulfilment costs are built. Weight handling and shipping fees are charged on the higher of actual weight or volumetric weight, where volumetric weight is length times breadth times height in centimetres divided by 5,000; standard-size items have a minimum chargeable weight of 500 g and are billed in 500 g increments, so an 800 g item to a regional address costs Rs 68 (Rs 51 plus Rs 17). Fulfilment centre fees: pick and pack Rs 17 per unit for standard items up to 1 kg, Rs 5 per extra kg up to 5 kg and Rs 2 per extra 5 kg after that, Rs 26 for heavy and bulky; storage Rs 50 per cubic foot per month; removals Rs 10 standard or Rs 30 expedited per unit, Rs 100 for heavy and bulky. Easy Ship uses flat fees by weight and distance: a 350 g headphone is Rs 55, a 3.5 kg item Rs 180. All fees exclude 18% GST. New Standard-level sellers are paid every 7 days, starting 7 days after delivery. Amazon's FBA page quotes a lower storage rate, so confirm in the fee calculator. How to apply: measure the packed box, compute volumetric weight before choosing packaging, and add 18% GST to every Amazon fee in the margin sheet.
